title: The First World Cup Kicked Off in Uruguay
summary: The inaugural FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, with the host nation going on to win the very first title.

contentBlocks.text: A tournament born in Montevideo

Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina 4-2 in the final at the newly built Estadio Centenario in Montevideo. Thirteen teams took part — mostly from the Americas, since the long sea voyage discouraged many European sides.

title: 1950 Had No Traditional Knockout Final
summary: The 1950 World Cup crowned its champion with a deciding match in a final group stage — there was no single knockout final like every other tournament.

contentBlocks.text: A final group, not a final match

Unlike every other World Cup, 1950 decided the title with a four-team final round-robin group rather than a single knockout final. Brazil only needed a draw against Uruguay in the last match to win the tournament outright.

Because Uruguay won that last match 2-1, it happened to also be the match that decided the championship — which is why it is still remembered as "the final" even though the format was a group, not a knockout tie.

title: Brazil Is the Only Ever-Present Team
summary: Brazil is the only men's national team to have qualified for and played in every FIFA World Cup since the first tournament in 1930.

contentBlocks.text: Never absent

Every World Cup since 1930 has featured Brazil — the only nation with a perfect qualification record across the tournament's entire history. Every other founding nation has missed at least one edition.

title: Miroslav Klose Is the World Cup's Top Scorer
summary: Germany's Miroslav Klose scored 16 goals across four World Cups (2002–2014), the most of any player in men's tournament history.

contentBlocks.text: Sixteen goals, four tournaments

Miroslav Klose overtook Ronaldo Nazário's mark of 15 World Cup goals during the 2014 tournament, finishing his career with 16 goals across the 2002, 2006, 2010, and 2014 editions — the all-time men's World Cup scoring record.

summary: Hosting for the first time since 1938, France won its first World Cup title in 1998, beating Brazil 3-0 in the final in Saint-Denis.

contentBlocks.text: Les Bleus at home
France hosted the 1998 World Cup and won its first title, beating defending champions Brazil 3-0 in the final at the Stade de France. Zinedine Zidane scored twice in the final.

summary: Spain won its only men's World Cup title in 2010, beating the Netherlands 1-0 after extra time in the final in Johannesburg.

title: Germany 7-1 Brazil: A World Cup Semi-Final Shock
summary: Germany thrashed host nation Brazil 7-1 in the 2014 World Cup semi-final, one of the most one-sided results in tournament history.

contentBlocks.text: Mineirazo

Playing in front of its own fans in Belo Horizonte, Brazil was stunned by Germany in the 2014 semi-final, conceding five goals in the first 29 minutes alone. Germany went on to win the tournament, beating Argentina in the final.
Germany's 7 goals set a new record for the most goals scored by a team in a men's World Cup semi-final.

title: Argentina Beat France on Penalties in a 2022 Final for the Ages
summary: Argentina won the 2022 World Cup on penalties after a 3-3 draw with France, capping Lionel Messi's career with his first World Cup title.

contentBlocks.text: A final with everything

The 2022 final in Qatar finished 3-3 after extra time, with Kylian Mbappé scoring a hat-trick for France and Lionel Messi scoring twice for Argentina. Argentina won the resulting penalty shootout 4-2 to claim its third World Cup title.

title: 2026 Will Be the First 48-Team World Cup
summary: The 2026 World Cup expands the tournament from 32 to 48 teams for the first time, the biggest format change since 1998.

contentBlocks.text: 32 becomes 48

The 2026 World Cup will feature 48 teams for the first time, up from 32 at every tournament since 1998. The expanded format uses 12 groups of four teams, with the top two from each group plus the eight best third-placed teams advancing to a new round of 32.

title: 2026 Is the First World Cup Hosted by Three Nations
summary: The 2026 World Cup is co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, the first men's World Cup shared by three countries.

contentBlocks.text: Three flags, one tournament

The United States, Canada, and Mexico are jointly hosting the 2026 World Cup, the first time a men's World Cup has been shared by three countries. Mexico becomes the first nation to host the men's tournament three times, after 1970 and 1986.

title: Only Two World Cup Finals Have Gone to Penalties
summary: In men's World Cup history, only the 1994 final (Brazil beat Italy) and the 2022 final (Argentina beat France) have been decided by a penalty shootout.

contentBlocks.text: Rare drama

Penalty shootouts have decided a men's World Cup final only twice: Brazil beat Italy 3-2 on penalties in 1994 after a scoreless draw, and Argentina beat France 4-2 on penalties in 2022 after a 3-3 draw.

title: Maradona's 1986 World Cup
summary: Diego Maradona led Argentina to the 1986 title, scoring the controversial 'Hand of God' goal and the celebrated 'Goal of the Century' in the same quarter-final.

contentBlocks.text: Two goals, four minutes apart

In the 1986 quarter-final against England, Diego Maradona scored twice in the space of four minutes: first an illegal handball he later called the 'Hand of God', then a mazy 60-metre solo run voted the 'Goal of the Century'. Argentina went on to win the tournament.
Maradona's handball goal was not overturned because the referees did not see the infringement — goal-line and video review did not exist in 1986.

title: Brazil 1970: The First Team to Win Three World Cups
summary: Brazil's 1970 squad, built around Pelé, became the first team to win three World Cups — a feat that let Brazil keep the original Jules Rimet Trophy permanently.

contentBlocks.text: Three titles, one trophy kept forever

Brazil's 1970 team — featuring Pelé, Jairzinho, Carlos Alberto, and Tostão — won the World Cup in Mexico, becoming the first nation to win the tournament three times (after 1958 and 1962). Under FIFA's rules at the time, that achievement let Brazil keep the original Jules Rimet Trophy permanently.

title: The Maracanã's 1950 Crowd — A Disputed Record
summary: The 1950 decider between Brazil and Uruguay is often cited as the largest crowd ever at a football match, though the exact attendance figure is disputed.

contentBlocks.text: How many people were really there?

The Brazil–Uruguay decider at the Maracanã in 1950 is widely cited as the largest crowd ever to watch a football match, with figures commonly quoted anywhere from about 173,000 to over 200,000. Because ticketing and counting methods from the era were inconsistent, historians have never settled on one official number — this fact is held back pending a source we're confident enough to publish as a specific figure.
